<!-- link1 "<B>MANAGEMENT&#146;S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF<BR>FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS</B>" -->
<DIV align="left"><A NAME="003"></A></DIV>

<P align="center"><B>MANAGEMENT&#146;S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF<BR>
FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS</B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>The following section of this Registration Statement contains certain
forward-looking statements that involve substantial risks and uncertainties.
When used in this section, the words &#147;anticipate,&#148; &#147;believe,&#148; &#147;estimate,&#148; and
&#147;expect&#148; and similar expressions as they relate to Reorganized Purina or its
management are intended to identify such forward-looking statements.
Reorganized Purina&#146;s actual results, performance or achievements could differ
materially from the results, performance or achievements expressed in, or
implied by, these forward-looking statements. Factors that could cause or
contribute to such differences include those discussed in &#147;Risk Factors&#148; and
elsewhere in this Registration Statement.</I>

<P align="left"><B>Overview</B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Old Purina&#146;s overall financial performance during 1999 was severely
impacted by the overall depressed conditions in the agriculture industry. This
is particularly evident in the swine industry where prices for market hogs
remain depressed. These depressed conditions resulted in a decrease of 32% in
volume of swine feed sales for the year December&nbsp;31, 1999.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In connection with the 1998 Merger, Old Purina incurred a significant
amount of indebtedness. See &#147;Business &#151; Background.&#148; Old Purina&#146;s substantial
degree of leverage limited its flexibility to adjust to the depressed
conditions in the agricultural industry and made it particularly vulnerable to
the downturn in the swine market. As a result of its financial condition
during 1999 and its substantial degree of leverage, Old Purina&#146;s ability to
finance its working capital requirements was adversely affected by its cash
requirements for debt service. On September&nbsp;15, 1999, Old Purina failed to
make a scheduled interest payment of $15.75&nbsp;million due to the holders of the
Senior Subordinated Notes. On October&nbsp;21, 1999, the Indenture Trustee for the
Senior Subordinated Notes accelerated such notes as a result of the failure to
make such interest payment. On September&nbsp;30, 1999, Old Purina failed to pay
$2.1&nbsp;million in principal payments under the Prepetition Credit Facility. Such
principal payment was subsequently made on October&nbsp;27, 1999. Old Purina
defaulted under both the Notes Indenture and the Prepetition Credit Facility.
Faced with these events and an inability to service future interest payment on
the Senior Subordinated Notes, Old Purina commenced the Reorganization Cases.
See &#147; &#151; Liquidity and Capital Resources.&#148;

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Reorganized Purina develops, manufactures and markets a comprehensive line
of animal nutrition products for dairy cattle, beef cattle, hogs, horses and
poultry, as well as specialty feeds for rabbits, zoo animals, birds, fish and
pets. For the year ended December&nbsp;31, 1999 the product mix by volume was
approximately 26% for dairy, 29% for beef cattle, 14% for hogs, 12% for horses,
7% for poultry and 12% for all others. The feed industry generally prices
products on the basis of aggregate ingredient cost plus a dollar amount margin,
rather than a gross profit percentage. As ingredient prices fluctuate, the
changes are generally passed on to customers through weekly changes in
Reorganized Purina&#146;s price lists. Feed tonnage and total income over
ingredient cost (&#147;IOIC&#148;), which is net sales minus cost of ingredients, and
gross profit (IOIC less manufacturing costs), rather than sales dollars, are
the key indicators of performance because of the distortions in sales dollars
caused by changes in commodity prices and product mix between complete feed and
concentrate products, to which customers add their own base ingredients, such
as corn and other grains. Historically, when the price of grains has been
relatively high, more of Old Purina&#146;s customers have tended to purchase
complete rations and Old Purina&#146;s sales volume has been higher; alternatively,
when the price of grains has been relatively low, more of Old Purina&#146;s
customers have tended to use their own grains and mix them with Old Purina&#146;s
higher-margin concentrates, resulting in lower sales volume but relatively
higher overall unit margins.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Reorganized Purina expects the U.S. feed industry to further consolidate
in the years ahead. Although the total volume of processed feed sold into the
commercial market segment may decline, larger producers are tending to purchase
products with lower inclusion rates and higher margins. As they grow larger,
these producers are typically better able to measure performance differences
and make sound economic decisions regarding nutrition and management programs.
Competition in the industry occasionally limits Reorganized Purina&#146;s ability to
pass ingredient price increases on to its customers; however, management
believes that Reorganized Purina&#146;s knowledge of the nutritional value of
ingredients and its sophisticated least-cost formulation system enable
Reorganized Purina to provide products that meet its nutritional standards and
maintain product quality while minimizing product cost.
<P align="center">14
<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>


<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The economic environment in the agricultural industry during 1998 and 1999
has been a difficult one for many individual producers and companies that
participate in the sector. Livestock commodity prices have been depressed and
reached historic lows in many markets. In addition to the overall economic
environment, there is significant continuing competition in all areas of
agriculture, including the feed industry.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Competition in the industry has caused Reorganized Purina and some of its
competitors to develop market and production risk arrangements for their
customers to promote sales. Old Purina entered into several production and
marketing joint venture arrangements with its animal production customers,
especially in the swine sector, in order to facilitate additional feed sales.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, to capitalize on the consolidation of the hog industry, Old
Purina implemented a strategy in 1997 that was expected to result in control
over the feeding of approximately six million market hogs over four years. The
program provides a source of high quality weanlings and feeder pigs (&#147;feeders&#148;)
to independent hog producers and gains the related feed business for Old
Purina. Under this program, at December&nbsp;31, 1999, Old Purina had future net
purchase commitments, subject to the counterparties&#146; ability to perform, to
acquire over 0.5&nbsp;million feeders over the next eight years. Approximately 37%
of these commitments are at fixed prices whereas the other 63% vary based on
current or published futures prices. The net purchase commitment of 0.5
million feeders represents gross commitments during such period for
approximately 3.7&nbsp;million feeders less 3.2&nbsp;million feeders which have
contractually been sold. These contractual sales are subject to the credit
worthiness of the third parties which may have deteriorated due to the
prolonged decline in the hog market.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Additionally, Reorganized Purina has direct ownership of several hog
operations which are expected to produce an additional 1.6&nbsp;million feeders over
the next ten years. As hog producers have been experiencing depressed market
prices for their end products, Reorganized Purina has significant exposure
relating to its feeder pig program, direct hog ownership and joint venture
interests in hog operations. At December&nbsp;31, 1999 and December&nbsp;31, 1998, Old
Purina had $8.6&nbsp;million and $10.3&nbsp;million, respectively, in hog inventory.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Based on published market prices at December&nbsp;31, 1999, Reorganized
Purina&#146;s net commitment to purchase the 0.5&nbsp;million feeders totals
approximately $17.0&nbsp;million. This is a decrease of $233.0&nbsp;million from such
amount at December&nbsp;31, 1998 due to the rejection of certain executory contracts
in accordance with Old Purina&#146;s Chapter&nbsp;11 bankruptcy filing totaling
approximately $139.0&nbsp;million, feeder purchases during the year, renegotiation
of future purchase agreements, additional contracts for the sale of feeders in
the future and the change in hog market prices. Upon receipt of the feeders,
Reorganized Purina can either sell them at current market prices, feed the pigs
at its owned or leased facilities, or contract with independent producers to
feed the pigs. Based on 1999 contractual commitments, estimated feed costs,
counterparty risks and current spot and futures prices, Reorganized Purina&#146;s loss in 2000 associated
with its swine exposure is estimated to be approximately $2.5 - 5.0&nbsp;million.
Depending on the future market price for both feeders and market hogs, any or
all of the options available to Reorganized Purina could have a significant
adverse impact on earnings, cash flows and liquidity.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;During 1999 Old Purina focused on managing and mitigating the impact of the
significant decline in hog prices on its performance. With the price of hogs
having increased moderately from December&nbsp;1998, which was the lowest price in
nearly forty years, and through the efforts of management, Old Purina mitigated
some of its swine exposure in an effort to reduce the negative implications on
future earnings, cash flow and liquidity. In April&nbsp;1999, Old Purina locked in
a margin on market hogs to be marketed during the remainder of 1999 by entering
into futures contracts for market hogs and the major feed ingredients to grow
the hogs. This action resulted in limiting the risk of any market decline for
the remainder of the year on these hogs, but also limited the potential for
gain if market prices significantly increased. Reorganized Purina has locked in
some, but not all, margin for hogs to be marketed in 2000 and, as such,
Reorganized Purina is subject to risk of further fluctuations in the price of
market hogs, which could have a material adverse impact on results of
operations and liquidity.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;During 1999, Old Purina made the decision to discontinue manufacturing
operations at five of its facilities. Products for distribution to customers of
the closed facilities are being manufactured at Reorganized Purina&#146;s other
facilities. In connection with these plant closures, Old Purina recorded a
loss of $13.1&nbsp;million on manufacturing assets, representing the amount by which
the book value exceeds the estimated net realized value. Estimated
<P align="center">15
<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>


<P>demolition
costs of $1.2&nbsp;million, severance costs of $0.4&nbsp;million and a write-off of $5.0
million for related goodwill were also recorded. Reorganized Purina will
continue to review the performance of its facilities in an attempt to optimize
overall capacity and maximize profits. This review may result in the decision
to discontinue operations at additional facilities which would result in an
additional loss provision being recorded.

<P align="left"><B>Results of Operations</B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<B><I>Year Ended December&nbsp;31, 1999 Compared to Year Ended December&nbsp;31, 1998</I></B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The overall economic environment in the agricultural industry during 1998
and 1999 has been a difficult one for many companies. Continued depressed
commodity prices and low market prices for producer products caused 1999 net
sales to decrease 11.7% from the 1998 period. While gross profit decreased
$12.0&nbsp;million or 6.4% from 1998 due primarily to increased competition in the
industry, the Company&#146;s gross profit percentage increased to 19.8% from 18.7%
due to production efficiencies. As a result, average feed IOIC per ton was
$63.73 for 1999, approximately equal to the amount for 1998. Overall volume
was 4.32&nbsp;million tons for the year 1999, a decrease of 6.7% from 1998.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Beef cattle and dairy cattle feed tons remained fairly constant in 1999 with
overall volume totaling 1.27&nbsp;million and 1.11&nbsp;million tons, respectively. Hog
volume decreased 32.4% reflecting the depressed market conditions for producers
and the loss of customers resulting from the consolidation within the hog industry.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Sales of horse feed remained strong as Old Purina increased its market
share with a volume increase of 12.3% during 1999 as total volume was just
under 0.50&nbsp;million tons. This increase continued the trend for the past seven
years as Old Purina&#146;s products continued to have strong customer acceptance.
Laying chicken and meatbird volume decreased 18.9% primarily as a result of a
major customer incurring severe financial difficulties and discontinuing any
purchases from Old Purina. Specialty and other volume increased 2.8% over 1998
as a result of continued emphasis on promotion of these products.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The decrease in overall volume caused a corresponding decrease in cost of
products sold. Ingredient costs decreased $101.8&nbsp;million and total cost of
products sold decreased $104.7&nbsp;million, or 12.9% from 1998. Manufacturing
costs also decreased $2.9&nbsp;million due to the lower 1999 volume and the
discontinuance or curtailment of manufacturing operations at five locations.
Marketing, distribution and advertising costs remained fairly constant as the
decrease in expense attributable to the volume decline was offset by continuing
costs associated with the ACS initiative. General and administrative expenses
were 7.4% of sales for 1999 as compared to 7.2% in 1998, excluding the $15.9
million expense in 1998 for compensation paid management and holders of options
and stock rights.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Amortization expense and research and development expenses, as a
percentage of sales, remained fairly constant as Old Purina continued its
emphasis on product developments.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;During 1999 Old Purina made the decision to discontinue or curtail
manufacturing operations at five of its facilities. Products for distribution
to customers of the closed facilities are being manufactured at Old Purina&#146;s
other facilities. In connection with these plant closures, Old Purina recorded
a loss of $13.1&nbsp;million on manufacturing assets, representing the amount by
which the book value exceeds estimated fair value. Estimated demolition costs
of $1.2&nbsp;million, severance costs of $0.4&nbsp;million and a write-off of $5.0
million for related goodwill were also recorded. Also, in 1999, Old Purina
recorded a provision for loss on impairment of intangible assets of $161.6
million. The provision reduces the carrying cost of intangible assets to
management&#146;s estimate of the fair value of intangible assets at December&nbsp;31,
1999. Management&#146;s estimate is based upon the expected net realizable value of
Purina Mills on a going concern basis, which contemplates continuity of
operations, realization of assets and liquidation of liabilities in the
ordinary course of business. However, as a result of the Chapter&nbsp;11 filings
and circumstances relating to this event, including Old Purina&#146;s highly
leveraged financial structure, such continuity of operations and realization of
assets and liquidation of liabilities is subject to significant uncertainty.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;During the third quarter of 1999, Old Purina conducted a comprehensive
strategic business review,
<P align="center">16
<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>


<P>including the development of a business plan which
addressed both short-term and longer-term issues required to stabilize and turn
around the business. See &#147;Business &#147; Business Plan and Strategy for
Reorganized Purina.&#148; In connection with the Business Plan and the
Reorganization Cases, Old Purina incurred advisory fees and expenses of $10.7
million during 1999. Additionally, Old Purina recorded severance costs of $3.9
million, bank fees of $1.4&nbsp;million and compensation expense of $2.1 in
connection with the KERP Program during 1999. These costs and fees are shown
as restructuring expenses.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Other (income)&nbsp;expense, net for 1999 relates to service fees for swine and
dairy management, the (income)&nbsp;loss of equity investments and losses on
marketing arrangements. The amount approximates the amount for 1998, excluding
the 1998 loss of $4.6&nbsp;million on the sale of discontinued products.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Interest expense for 1999 increased $1.2&nbsp;million as a result of the
increase in the outstanding debt under the Prepetition Credit Facility. The
1999 provision for income taxes, in addition to not recording a tax
benefit for 1999 losses, reflects the establishment of a valuation
allowance on Old Purina&#146;s deferred tax assets. There is no assurance that the deferred tax
assets or tax benefit of 1999 losses would be realized considering the
bankruptcy filing and the expected discontinuance of its tax sharing agreement
with Koch Industries. The 1998 effective income tax rate approximates the
statutory rate.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<B><I>Year Ended December&nbsp;31, 1998 Compared to Year Ended December&nbsp;31, 1997</I></B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Due to overall lower commodity prices, net sales decreased 11.5% from the
1997 period. Gross profit decreased $28.3&nbsp;million in 1998, or 13.1% from 1997.
Overall volume was 4.63&nbsp;million tons for the year ended December&nbsp;31, 1998, a
1.6% decrease from 1997. The decrease in volume was attributable to a decrease
in animal numbers, extreme depressed prices for end products of producers and
continued consolidation in the hog industry. Average feed IOIC per ton was
$63.66 for 1998, a 2.2% decrease from the prior year. The decrease in average
feed IOIC per ton was attributable to intense competition, low commodity prices
and the depressed agriculture economy.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Beef cattle feed tons remained consistent with the 1997 period, although the
Company experienced intense competition for the cattle feed business. Dairy
cattle feed  tons decreased 4.2% due to some product mix switch to concentrates and a
decrease in the number of smaller dairy operations. Hog volume decreased 3.9%
due to the depressed market conditions and the resulting pressure on hog feed
margins.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Horse feed  volume increased 8.4% over the 1998 period. The success in growing
this business was the result of continued aggressive promotion of products.
Laying chicken and meatbird feed  volume decreased 11.9% from 1997. The decrease can
be attributed to the loss of sales of lower margin turkey and broiler feed to
two large customers. Specialty and other volume increased 3.2% over 1997.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Cost of products sold decreased $101.4&nbsp;million, or 11.1% from 1997, due
primarily to the $122.1&nbsp;million decrease in ingredient costs. This decrease
was partially offset by 1998 net losses of $13.8&nbsp;million from Old Purina&#146;s hog
program due to the severely depressed hog market. Manufacturing expenses
increased $6.9&nbsp;million over the 1997 period due primarily to increased
depreciation expense and other costs associated with the opening of the new
Lubbock mill in the fourth quarter of 1998. Marketing, distribution and
advertising costs increased $3.3&nbsp;million from 1997 due primarily to an increase
in the sales force and costs associated with the roll out of the ACS
initiative. General and administrative expenses increased $31.8&nbsp;million
primarily due to the $15.9&nbsp;million of compensation paid to management and
holders of options and stock rights units as a part of the 1998 Merger, an
increase in the provision for bad debt losses on capital loans and trade
receivables of $10.2&nbsp;million and $5.0&nbsp;million attributable to increased
information system costs and relocation and severance costs. The additional
bad debt provision is primarily related to customers in the hog industry.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Amortization of intangibles and research and development costs remained
consistent with the 1997 period.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The provision for loss on guarantees of $14.2&nbsp;million includes an $11.5
million charge for a guarantee Old Purina had to an entity that provided
funding for Old Purina&#146;s network of independently- owned dealers and producers.
The remaining $2.7&nbsp;million relates to loan guarantees made to banks to assist
the Old Purina Companies&#146;
<P align="center">17
<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>


<P>customers in obtaining bank loans for working
capital, lines of credit, and additions to property, plant and equipment.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Other (income)&nbsp;expense, net for 1998 relates to service fees for swine and
dairy management, the (income)&nbsp;loss on Old Purina&#146;s equity investments, losses
on marketing arrangements and losses on the sale of discontinued products. An
increase in service fees of $1.1&nbsp;million over 1997 was offset by losses on
marketing arrangements of $5.9&nbsp;million due primarily to the depressed
conditions prevailing in the hog market. Additionally, Old Purina incurred a
charge of $4.6&nbsp;million in 1998 on the sale of discontinued products and a
charge of $1.0&nbsp;million in 1997 related to an aborted recapitalization project.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Interest expense for 1998 increased $6.0&nbsp;million as a result of the
increase in the outstanding debt under the Prepetition Credit Facility and the
Senior Subordinated Notes. Old Purina&#146;s effective income tax rate in 1998
approximated the statutory rate. Old Purina&#146;s effective income tax rate
exceeded the statutory rate in 1997 due to amortization of goodwill not being
allowed as a tax deduction. Management reviewed the realization of the
deferred tax assets at December&nbsp;31, 1998 and believed it was more likely than
not that they would be realized through future taxable earnings.

<P align="left"><B>Liquidity and Capital Resources</B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For the year ended December&nbsp;31 1999, net cash used in operating activities
was $32.0&nbsp;million compared to $19.8&nbsp;million net cash provided during the same
period in 1998. The increase in net cash used results primarily from the
reduction in payables of $31.8&nbsp;million, a reduction in advance payments of $6.4
million and an $11.6&nbsp;million increase in the cash operating loss.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Net cash used in investing activities was $23.3&nbsp;million and $28.7&nbsp;million
for the years ended December&nbsp;31, 1999 and 1998, respectively. This change was
due to a decrease in capital expenditures of $8.8&nbsp;million as construction of
the Lubbock, Texas plant was completed in the last quarter of 1998. This
decrease was partially offset by an increase in capital loans over the
comparable 1998 period.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Net cash provided by financing activities in 1999 includes borrowings on
the Prepetition Credit Facility of $67.5&nbsp;million less the term loan repayment
of $5.5&nbsp;million. Net cash provided by financing activities in 1998 includes
the proceeds from the Prepetition Credit Facility of $220.0&nbsp;million, the
proceeds from the Senior Subordinated Notes of $350.0&nbsp;million less the
repayment of certain prior indebtedness totaling $388.7&nbsp;million and payments of
$253.3&nbsp;million, including $8.0&nbsp;million acquisition costs, for the purchase of
PM Holdings shares in connection with the 1998 Merger. In addition, net cash
used in financing activities in 1998 includes payments of $12.4&nbsp;million for
financing costs.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In connection with filing Old Purina&#146;s Reorganization Cases, Old Purina
obtained debtor in possession financing to ensure sufficient liquidity to meet
ongoing operating needs. In November, 1999, Old Purina obtained Bankruptcy
Court approval for borrowings up to $50&nbsp;million under the Revolving Credit and
Guarantee Agreement (the &#147;DIP Credit Agreement&#148;). Under the DIP Credit
Agreement, Old Purina was permitted to borrow at the bank&#146;s alternative base
rate plus 2% or, at Old Purina&#146;s option, the London inter-bank offered rate
plus 3%. The obligations of Old Purina under the DIP Credit Agreement were
guaranteed by PM Holdings Corporation and certain Old Purina subsidiaries.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;At December&nbsp;31, 1999, Old Purina had $48.1&nbsp;million in cash and cash
equivalents on hand with no amount available for borrowing under the
Prepetition Credit Facility. However, $49.1&nbsp;million was available for
borrowing under the DIP Credit Agreement. Old Purina has
operated with a relatively low working capital level because a majority of its
sales are made on terms whereby customers receive a 3% discount if payment is
received immediately upon shipment of feed products, and raw ingredients are
normally purchased just prior to manufacturing and shipment.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Old Purina&#146;s capital expenditures during fiscal year 1999 were
approximately $21.0&nbsp;million, which includes $3.3&nbsp;million related to the new
accounting and information reporting system.

<P align="center">18
<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>


<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Under the Plan, on the Effective Date holders of prepetition credit
facility notes will receive, among other things, their pro rata share of new
debt instruments under a new term loan credit agreement (the &#147;Reinstated Credit
Agreement&#148;). The Reinstated Credit Agreement is expected to be $225&nbsp;million in
principal amount, $175&nbsp;million of which will be Tranche A notes and $50&nbsp;million
of which will be Tranche B notes. Tranche A notes will bear interest per annum
at the alternative base rate plus an applicable margin (ranging from 1.75% to
2.50%) or, at Reorganized Purina&#146;s option, the London interbank offered rate
plus an applicable margin (ranging from 2.75% to 3.50%). Interest will be
payable monthly in arrears. The Tranche A notes will mature on December&nbsp;31,
2003. The Tranche B notes will mature on December&nbsp;31, 2002. The obligations
of Reorganized Purina under the Reinstated Credit Agreement will be guaranteed
by certain subsidiaries of Reorganized Purina.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Under the Plan, on the Effective Date Reorganized Purina will enter into a
$50&nbsp;million revolving exit financing facility (the &#147;Exit Financing Facility&#148;)
with certain senior lenders for working capital, capital expenditures and new
letters of credit. Reorganized Purina will be permitted to issue up to $30
million letters of credit under the Exit Financing Facility. Holders of
prepetition and postpetition letters of credit will be issued new letters of
credit under the Exit Financing Facility. Loans under the Exit Financing
Facility are expected to bear interest per annum at the London interbank
offered rate plus 2.75%. Interest will be payable monthly in arrears.
Reorganized Purina will also incur a facility fee of $500,000 and will be
required to pay a commitment fee of 0.50% per annum on the unused amount of the
Exit Financing Facility. The Exit Financing Facility will mature thirty months
from its inception. The obligations of Reorganized Purina under the Exit
Financing Facility will be guaranteed by certain subsidiaries of Reorganized
Purina.

<P align="left"><B>Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosure About Market Risk</B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Loans under the Reinstated Credit Agreement and the Exit Financing
Facility bear interest at floating rates which are, at Reorganized Purina&#146;s
option, based either upon bank prime or Eurodollar rates. Reorganized Purina
expects to primarily pay interest based on the three month London interbank offered rate plus an applicable margin ranging from 2.75% to 3.5%. As a
result, Reorganized Purina will be subject to interest rate risk. To mitigate
the impact of fluctuations in interest rates, Reorganized Purina intends to continue to utilize
interest rate swaps and collars to fix the rate on its floating rate debt.

<P align="left"><B>Recently Issued Statements of Financial Accounting Standards</B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In June&nbsp;1998 the Financial Accounting Standards Board issued Statement of
Financial Accounting Standards No.&nbsp;133 (SFAS No.&nbsp;133), Accounting for
Derivative Instruments and Hedging Activities. This statement standardizes the
accounting for derivative instruments by requiring that an entity recognize
these items as assets and liabilities in the statement of financial position
and measure them at fair value. SFAS No.&nbsp;133 becomes effective for fiscal
years beginning after June&nbsp;15, 2000. Reorganized Purina is currently
evaluating the impact of SFAS No.&nbsp;133 on its financial statements.

<!-- link1 "<B>PROPERTIES</B>" -->
<DIV align="left"><A NAME="004"></A></DIV>
<P align="center"><B>PROPERTIES</B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Reorganized Purina owns its corporate headquarters in St. Louis and a
1,188 acre research center in Gray Summit, Missouri.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Reorganized Purina expects to operate 48 or fewer feed manufacturing
plants located in 25 states, one of which is leased. In addition to on-site
storage at each of their manufacturing plants, Reorganized Purina also stores
products in owned or leased warehouses.

<P>Mr.&nbsp;Dumler has been a Director of Old Purina since March&nbsp;1999. From April&nbsp;1999
through February&nbsp;2000, he also served as part of the three-member Office of the
Chief Executive Officer of Old Purina. Prior thereto, he was Executive Vice
President, Corporate Finance for Koch Industries. He joined Koch Industries in
1989 and has served in various management positions, including Vice President,
Chemicals Group and Chief Financial Officer, Gas Liquids Group.

<P>Mr.&nbsp;Durkin is Director, Corporate Services &#38; Projects for Koch Industries and
has been a Director of Old Purina since March&nbsp;1999. From April&nbsp;1999 through
February&nbsp;2000, he also served as part of the three-member Office of the Chief
Executive Officer of Old Purina. He joined Koch Industries in 1982 and has
served in various operating and marketing capacities, including several
operating Vice President roles and President of the former Minerals Division.

<P>Mr.&nbsp;Knudson has been a Director of Old Purina since March&nbsp;1999 and is the sole
director and President of PM Holdings. From April&nbsp;1999 through February&nbsp;2000,
he also served as part of the three-member Office of the Chief Executive
Officer of Old Purina. Previously, he was Group Controller for Koch Industries
Agriculture Group. He joined Koch Industries in 1980 and has held various
financial management positions, including Assistant Controller for Koch
Industries and Group Controller for Koch Refining, Koch Energy and Koch
Chemical.

<P>Mr.&nbsp;Kerbs has been President of Old Purina since August&nbsp;1999 and Chief
Executive Officer of Old Purina since February&nbsp;2000. From August&nbsp;1999 through
February&nbsp;2000, he acted as Old Purina&#146;s Chief Operating Officer. Previously,
he was Executive Vice President of Old Purina beginning in August&nbsp;1998. He
joined Old Purina in 1969 and has served in various operational,
administrative, marketing and management positions.

<!-- PAGEBREAK -->

<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>



<P>Mr.&nbsp;Hoogmoed has been Old Purina&#146;s Executive Vice President, Livestock
Production Systems Business Group since February&nbsp;2000. From August&nbsp;1999
through February&nbsp;2000, he was Senior Vice President, Livestock Production
Systems at Old Purina. He joined Old Purina in 1979 and previously has served
in various positions, including District Manager, Division Sales Manager,
Regional Director of Sales and Marketing, Area General Manager, Central Region
Vice President; and, most recently, Vice President, Swine Operations.

<P>Mr.&nbsp;Swank has been Chief Financial Officer of Old Purina since April&nbsp;1998 and
an Executive Vice President of Old Purina since February&nbsp;2000. In these roles,
he currently leads Old Purina&#146;s integrated Finance, Control/Tax and Risk
Management Business Capability Group. Prior to his appointment as Chief
Financial Officer of Old Purina, he was Chief Financial Officer of Koch
Agriculture, a position he held since January&nbsp;1997. Before joining Koch
Agriculture, he was a management consultant with Deloitte Consulting, L.L.C.

<P>Mr.&nbsp;Kabbes joined Old Purina as General Counsel and Secretary in March&nbsp;1999.
He has been an Executive Vice President of Old Purina since February&nbsp;2000. In
these roles, he currently has responsibility for Old Purina&#146;s integrated Human
Resources, Legal and Public Relations Business Capability Group. Prior to
joining Old Purina, he was an attorney for Koch Industries. Prior to joining
Koch Industries in July&nbsp;1997, he was a partner in the Chicago, Illinois law
firm of Schiff Hardin &#38; Waite.

<P>Mr.&nbsp;Emanuelson joined Old Purina in July&nbsp;1998 and has been Old Purina&#146;s Chief
Information Officer since August&nbsp;1999 and an Executive Vice President of Old
Purina since February&nbsp;2000. In these roles, he currently is responsible for
Old Purina&#146;s Information Technology organization. Prior to joining Old Purina,
he was employed by Compaq Computer Corporation for seven years, where he held
various positions, including Director of Corporate Manufacturing Systems.

<P>Mr.&nbsp;Schu has been a Vice President of Old Purina since August&nbsp;1998 and became
Old Purina&#146;s Executive Vice President, Dealer Business Group in February&nbsp;2000.
He joined Old Purina in 1980 and has served in various positions, including
field sales, sales management, Director, Retail Specialty Business Group and
Vice President, National Dealer Sales.

<P>Mr.&nbsp;Bowen has been a Vice President of Old Purina since October&nbsp;1995 and became
Old Purina&#146;s Executive Vice President, Operations in February&nbsp;2000. He joined
Old Purina in 1984 and has served in various positions, including Manager
Financial Services, District Manager, Division Sales Manager, Region Director
of Pricing, Area General Manager, and Vice President, Dairy Operations.

<P>Mr.&nbsp;Meinz has been Vice President, Treasurer and Controller of Old Purina since
August&nbsp;1998. He joined Old Purina in February&nbsp;1988 as Director of Taxes and
was promoted to Controller in September&nbsp;1993.

<P>There are no family relationships between any of the above-named executive
officers and directors.

exploration and development company.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Mr.&nbsp;Cummings will become a Director of Reorganized Purina as of the Effective

that date until his retirement in 1998 as a General Partner of the firm.
Since his retirement, Mr.&nbsp;Cummings has served as an Advisory Director of Goldman Sachs &amp; Co.

1994. Mr.&nbsp;Hamwee was previously associated with The Blackstone Group, where he
worked on a wide range of assignments in the Merchant Banking, Mergers &#38;
Acquisitions and Restructuring departments.

officers and directors.

<P align="left"><B>Reorganized Purina Board of Directors</B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Under the Delaware General Corporation Law (the &#147;DGCL&#148;), the business and
affairs of Reorganized Purina will be managed under the direction of the Board
of Directors of Reorganized Purina, which will initially consist of five
members.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Amended Certificate and the Amended By-Laws will provide that the size
of the Board of Directors will be established from time to time only (a)&nbsp;by an
affirmative vote of a majority of the total number of directors that
Reorganized Purina would have if there were no vacancies on the Board of
Directors or (b)&nbsp;by the affirmative vote of the holders of a majority of the
voting stock, voting together as a single class, except as may be provided in
any designation containing the express terms of preferred stock to be issued
pursuant to resolution of the Board of Directors (a &#147;Preferred Stock
Designation&#148;); <I>provided, however, </I>that the number of directors shall not be
less than five nor more than nine except as may be provided in any Preferred
Stock Designation. When so fixed, such number shall continue to be the
authorized number of directors until changed by the stockholders or directors.
<P align="center">24
<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>


<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Except as provided otherwise in any Preferred Stock Designation, directors
may be elected by the stockholders (a)&nbsp;at an annual meeting of stockholders or
(b)&nbsp;if no annual meeting is held or if an annual meeting is held but directors
are not elected, at a special meeting of stockholders called for that purpose.
Neither the holding of a special meeting of stockholders nor the election of
directors at a special meeting of stockholders will, by itself, shorten the
term of any incumbent director. Except as may be provided in any Preferred
Stock Designation, any vacancy that occurs on the Board of Directors, including
any vacancy that results from an increase in the number of directors and any
vacancy that results from death, resignation, disqualification, removal or
other cause, may be filled only (i)&nbsp;by the affirmative vote of a majority of
the remaining directors then in office, even though less than a quorum of the
Board of Directors, or by a sole remaining director or (ii)&nbsp;by the affirmative
vote of the stockholders after a vote to increase the number of directors at a
meeting called for that purpose. Any director elected to fill a vacancy
created by the death, resignation, disqualification or removal of an incumbent
director will hold office for the remainder of the term of such incumbent
directors.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Pursuant to the Amended By-Laws, no annual meeting of stockholders will be
held in 2000. The first annual meeting of the stockholders of Reorganized
Purina will be held in 2001 at such time and on such business day as
Reorganized Purina&#146;s Board of Directors determines.

<P align="left"><B>Board Committees</B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Amended By-Laws provide that Reorganized Purina&#146;s Board of Directors
may establish an Executive Committee or any other committees as it may from
time to time determine are necessary. Reorganized Purina contemplates that the
Board of Directors may establish an Executive Committee and will establish an
Audit Committee and a Compensation Committee as of or promptly after the
Effective Date. The composition of such committees has not been determined,
but the membership of the Audit Committee will be comprised of at least three
independent directors, and Reorganized Purina expects that the members of the
Compensation Committee will be non-employee directors. Under the Amended
By-Laws, a committee will possess and may exercise all of the power and
authority granted to it by the Board of Directors consistent with the DGCL,
provided that such committees may not fill vacancies among the directors or any
committee thereof.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;If Reorganized Purina&#146;s Board of Directors establishes an Executive
Committee, such committee will possess and may exercise, subject to the control
and direction of the Board of Directors, all the powers of the Board of
Directors in the management and control of the business of Reorganized Purina,
regardless of whether such powers are specifically conferred by the Amended
By-Laws; <I>provided, however, </I>that the Executive Committee will have no right to
(a)&nbsp;approve a merger or consolidation of Reorganized Purina with or into any
other entity or any other material business combination transaction involving
Reorganized Purina or any of its significant subsidiaries, (b)&nbsp;authorize the
sale of all or substantially all of the assets of Reorganized Purina or (c)
fill any vacancies on the Executive Committee or the Board of Directors.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Audit Committee, in accordance with a charter to be adopted prior to
the Effective Date, is expected to review: (a)&nbsp;the professional services to be
provided by Reorganized Purina&#146;s independent auditors and the independence of
such firm from management of Reorganized Purina; (b)&nbsp;the scope of the audit by
Reorganized Purina&#146;s independent auditors; (c)&nbsp;the annual financial statements
of Reorganized Purina; (d)&nbsp;Reorganized Purina&#146;s systems of internal accounting
controls; and (e)&nbsp;such other matters with respect to the accounting, auditing
and financial reporting practices and procedures of Reorganized Purina as it
may find appropriate or as may be brought to its attention.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Compensation Committee is expected to: (a)&nbsp;review executive salaries;
(b)&nbsp;administer the bonus, incentive compensation and equity incentive plans of
Reorganized Purina; and (c)&nbsp;approve the salaries and other benefits of the
executive officers of Reorganized Purina. See &#147;Executive Compensation &#151;
Employee Benefit Matters &#151; Existing Benefit Programs and Agreements&#148; and &#147; &#151;
New Benefit Programs.&#148; In addition, the Compensation Committee is expected to
advise and consult with Reorganized Purina&#146;s management regarding pension and
other benefit plans and compensation policies and practices of Reorganized
Purina.


<P align="center">25
<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>
<P align="left"><B>Director Nomination Procedures</B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Amended By-Laws provide that nominations for election of directors,
except as may be otherwise provided in any Preferred Stock Designation, will be
made at a meeting of stockholders by or at the direction of the Board of
Directors of Reorganized Purina, or by any stockholder who has complied with
the applicable nomination procedures contained in the Amended By-Laws. The
Amended By-Laws require that a stockholder&#146;s notice of intent to nominate
candidates for election as directors must be delivered to or mailed and
received at the principal executive offices of Reorganized Purina, in the case
of a special meeting, at the time of the request for the meeting, or, in the
case of an annual meeting, not less than 60&nbsp;days, nor more than 90&nbsp;days, prior
to (a)&nbsp;the date of the first annual meeting following the Effective Date or (b)
with respect to subsequent annual meetings, the date on which Reorganized
Purina first mailed its proxy materials for the prior year&#146;s annual meeting of
stockholders; <I>provided, however, </I>that, if the annual meeting is called for a
date that is not within 30&nbsp;days before or after the anniversary of the prior
year&#146;s annual meeting, notice by the stockholder in order to be timely must be
so received no later than the close of business on the tenth calendar day
following the day on which public disclosure of the date of the annual meeting
was made. The Amended By-Laws further require that the notice by the
stockholder set forth certain information concerning such stockholder and the
stockholder&#146;s nominees, including their names and addresses; proof that such
stockholder is entitled to vote at such meeting; the class and number of shares
of Reorganized Purina owned or beneficially owned by such stockholder and the
stockholder&#146;s nominees; any agreements between the relevant parties pursuant to
which the nomination is to be made; such other information as would be required
to be included in a proxy statement soliciting proxies for the election of the
nominees of such stockholder; and the consent of each nominee to serve as a
director of Reorganized Purina, if so elected. The chairman of the meeting may
refuse to acknowledge the nomination of any person not made in compliance with
these requirements.

<P align="left"><B>Compensation Committee Interlocks and Insider Participation</B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Since its acquisition by Koch Industries in 1998, Old Purina has not had a
Compensation Committee or other committee of the Board of Directors performing
similar functions. Previously, decisions concerning compensation of executive
officers of Old Purina were made by Old Purina&#146;s Chief Executive Officer or its
Board of Directors. The Board of Directors of Reorganized Purina will
establish a Compensation Committee effective as of the Effective Date. See &#147;
&#151; Board Committees.&#148;

<P align="left"><B>Director Compensation</B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Each non-employee director of Reorganized Purina will be compensated
subsequent to the Effective Date in a manner to be determined by the
Reorganized Purina Board.

<P align="left"><B>Employee Benefit Matters</B>

<P align="left"><B><I>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Existing Benefit Programs</I></B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Old Purina&#146;s employees participated in various retirement and welfare
plans administered by Koch Industries, subject to reimbursement to Koch
Industries by Old Purina for the cost of such participation. Effective January
1, 2000, Old Purina ceased participating in all of Koch Industries&#146; benefit
plans and adopted new stand-alone plans, which are sponsored and administered
by Reorganized Purina. The following discussion summarizes the principal terms
of the current plans effective January&nbsp;1, 2000. See &#147;Executive Compensation &#151;
Employee Benefit Matters &#151; New Benefit Programs&#148; for a description of benefit
plans to be adopted by Reorganized Purina on the Effective Date.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>Savings Plan.</I>&nbsp;Old Purina established a new 401(k) plan effective January
1, 2000 under which employees are eligible to make before-tax and after-tax
contributions. Old Purina makes matching contributions (up to 6% of pay) to
the new plan. The new plan accepted a transfer of assets and liabilities from
the Koch Industries&#146; savings plans which covered the Purina employees prior to
January&nbsp;1, 2000.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>Pension Plans.</I>&nbsp;Certain union employees of Old Purina participate in the
Purina Mills, Inc. Retirement Plan for Production Employees (the &#147;Purina
Pension Plan&#148;), a defined benefit pension plan previously sponsored by Old
Purina. Benefits under the Purina Pension Plan are based on a formula that
takes into account service and final average pay.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Other union employees of Reorganized Purina participate in a
multi-employer pension plan. Prior to January&nbsp;1, 2000, Koch Industries made
contributions to this plan on behalf of the covered employees. Old Purina
reimbursed Koch Industries for these contributions. Old Purina began making
these contributions directly to the multi-employer pension plan on January&nbsp;1,
2000.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Pursuant to an indemnity agreement with the Koch Entities (the &#147;Koch
Indemnity Agreement&#148;), Reorganized Purina has agreed to indemnify the Koch
Entities with respect to any possible liabilities under Title IV of ERISA
relating to these pension plans. See &#147;Certain Relationship and Related
Transactions&#148;.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>The CAP Plan.</I>&nbsp;Prior to 1994, certain executives of Old Purina elected to
defer certain bonuses under a capital appreciation plan (&#147;the CAP Plan&#148;).
Executives who made such deferrals are entitled to receive retirement and death
benefits under the CAP Plan. Prior to the Petition Date, benefits under the
CAP Plan were paid by Koch Industries, and Old Purina reimbursed Koch
Industries for the cost of these benefits. As of December&nbsp;31, 1999, the
projected benefit obligations under the CAP Plan were $24.0&nbsp;million. For the
year ended December&nbsp;31, 1999, the annual benefit payments under the CAP Plan
amounted to $1.1&nbsp;million.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;To assist Old Purina in meeting its obligations under the CAP Plan, Old
Purina purchased corporate-owned life insurance (&#147;COLI&#148;) on the lives of CAP
Plan participants. Old Purina pays the annual premiums on these policies in
the amount of $1.2&nbsp;million. The COLI policies are held in an irrevocable
grantor trust. Under the terms of the trust, the trust assets are required to
be held by the trustee for the benefit of Old Purina&#146;s creditors in the event
of Old Purina&#146;s insolvency. The gross cash surrender value of the COLI
policies as of December&nbsp;31, 1999 was approximately $15.4&nbsp;million.
<P align="center">28
<!-- PAGEBREAK -->
<P><HR noshade><P>
<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>


<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>Health and Welfare Benefits.</I>&nbsp;Old Purina established various stand-alone
health and welfare plans effective January&nbsp;1, 2000.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In addition, Reorganized Purina sponsors two &#147;voluntary employee benefits
association&#148; (&#147;VEBA&#148;) trusts, which are used to pay the claims under a
self-insured medical plan and a self-insured long-term disability plan, both of
which were frozen effective May&nbsp;31, 1998. As of December&nbsp;31, 1999, the VEBA
trusts contained assets of approximately $.8&nbsp;million. Reorganized Purina
intends to reactivate the VEBA trust for the medical plan and use its assets to
pay for benefits under the stand-alone Reorganized Purina medical plan
effective January&nbsp;1, 2000.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>Retiree Medical Benefits.</I>&nbsp;Reorganized Purina retirees meeting certain age
and service requirements are eligible for retiree medical benefits. In
connection with the Plan, Koch Industries agreed to continue to provide retiree
medical benefits for pre-2000 retirees through the completion of three-year
transition period under the 1998 Merger, subject to reimbursement by
Reorganized Purina of up to $150,000. Post-1999 retirees will be offered
retiree medical benefits, at the retirees&#146; expense, under the stand-alone
Reorganized Purina medical plan.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>Retiree Life Insurance Benefits.</I>&nbsp;Certain former employees of Old Purina
were receiving life insurance coverage under various term insurance contracts,
the premiums of which were being paid by Old Purina. Reorganized Purina will
continue to be obligated to pay these retiree benefits to the extent required
by section 1114(a) of the Bankruptcy Code.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>Key Employee Retention Program.</I>&nbsp;Old Purina adopted the KERP Program in
September&nbsp;1999. The KERP Program was designed to attract, retain and provide
incentives to directors and key employees during Old Purina&#146;s financial and
business restructuring. Reorganized Purina believes that the KERP Program will
continue to be critical to its ability to attract and retain key employees
following the Effective Date. Old Purina obtained authority to continue and
implement the KERP Program, subject to certain modifications. The KERP
Program, as modified, includes the following four principal components:

<P>
<TABLE width="100%" border="0" cellpadding="0" cellspacing="0">
<TR>
        <TD width="3%"></TD>

<TR valign="top">
        <TD>&nbsp;</TD>
        <TD>(a)&nbsp;<U>Retention/Stay Bonuses.</U>&nbsp;The KERP Program authorizes the
payment of retention bonuses to approximately 190 key employees.
Executive level employees are not eligible for this bonus. The
amount of each bonus generally is based on a percentage of base
salary. Depending on the classification of an employee, a specified
percentage of the retention bonus is earned on one, two or four
specified dates between the period from December&nbsp;31, 1999 and
December&nbsp;31, 2000. Employees must be employed on these &#147;earn-in&#148;
dates (or be terminated without cause prior to such dates) to
receive payment of a retention bonus. Retention bonuses are
projected not to exceed $4.4&nbsp;million in the aggregate.</TD>
</TR>
<TR>
        <TD>&nbsp;</TD>
</TR>
<TR valign="top">
        <TD>&nbsp;</TD>
        <TD>(b)&nbsp;<U>Annual Incentive Payments.</U>&nbsp;The KERP Program revised the
financial forecasts and targets of Old Purina&#146;s annual incentive
program for 1999. Approximately 250 employees were eligible for
annual incentive payments in 1999. As revised, employees were
eligible for target incentive payments depending on the attainment
of specified revised company and individual goals. These goals were
modified to reflect the impact of Old Purina&#146;s reorganization. For
example, under the revised program, (i)&nbsp;employees were eligible to
earn the individual component of their annual incentive payments
whether or not Old Purina&#146;s goals are met and (ii)&nbsp;Old Purina&#146;s
target adjusted earnings before interest, taxes and depreciation was
lowered for 1999. The amount of such payments, which were paid on

top management positions are eligible to receive emergence bonuses
based primarily upon Old Purina&#146;s successful reorganization.</TD>

<P><I>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Severance Pay Plan.</I>&nbsp;Old Purina adopted a formal severance plan (the
&#147;Severance Pay Plan&#148;), which became effective on November&nbsp;1, 1999. The formal
plan implemented Old Purina&#146;s unwritten severance pay policy. The Severance
Pay Plan was designed to attract, retain and provide incentives to employees
during Old Purina&#146;s financial and business restructuring. The Severance Pay
Plan covers all employees of Reorganized Purina. Under the Severance Pay Plan,
Reorganized Purina has the discretion to pay severance benefits to employees
who are involuntarily terminated without cause. In general, severance pay will
be paid in the amount of one week&#146;s pay for each year of service, plus an
additional $1,000. Reorganized Purina retains the right to increase or
decrease the amount of these payments. Old Purina paid approximately $2.6
million in severance pay for the period from July&nbsp;1, 1999 through December&nbsp;31,
1999.

<P><I>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Employment Agreements.</I>&nbsp;Old Purina has entered into employment agreements
with 23 senior executives. The employment agreements for 22 of these senior
executives are substantially identical (collectively, the &#147;Senior Executive
Agreements&#148;). These executives will serve Reorganized Purina under their
respective Senior Executive Agreements for an initial period of two years from
September&nbsp;1999, with an automatic yearly extension thereafter, unless the
employer or the executive has given written notice of termination not less than
90&nbsp;days prior to the yearly renewal date.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The Senior Executive Agreements set forth (a)&nbsp;the executive&#146;s compensation
and benefits, (b)&nbsp;the executive&#146;s obligations not to compete for the term of
the agreement plus one year (if the termination is not in connection with a
&#147;triggering event&#148;) or two years (if the termination is in connection with a
triggering event) unless the executive terminated his employment for good
reason or the employer terminates the executive for good cause and (c)&nbsp;the
executive&#146;s right to receive severance payments if the agreement is terminated.
For purposes of the Senior Executive Agreements, triggering events included a
change in control or the insolvency of Old Purina. Old Purina&#146;s chapter 11
filings constituted a triggering event under the Senior Executive Agreements.
If an executive is terminated by Reorganized Purina without good cause and not
in connection with a triggering event, the executive will receive a severance
payment in the amount of the executive&#146;s annual base salary. If an executive
is terminated by Reorganized Purina without good cause or terminates his
employment for good reason and, in either case, in connection with a triggering
event, the executive will receive a severance payment in the amount of either
one or two times the executive&#146;s annual base salary (depending on the position
of the executive), plus either one or two times the amount of the executive&#146;s
larger annual incentive bonus for the past two years. However, severance
payments under the Senior Executive Agreements will not exceed the limits
contained in section 280G of the Internal Revenue Code. Finally, if an
executive&#146;s employment is terminated in connection with a triggering event and
the executive becomes entitled to severance pay under the applicable Senior
Executive Agreement, Reorganized Purina will either continue the executive&#146;s
medical and dental benefits or pay the executive for equivalent medical and
dental coverage until the earlier of (i)&nbsp;one or two years from the date of
termination (depending on the position of the executive) or (ii)&nbsp;the date such
coverage is replaced by new coverage obtained by the executive or the
executive&#146;s spouse.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The prepetition employment agreement with Mr.&nbsp;Swank, Executive Vice
President and Chief Financial Officer of Old Purina (the &#147;Prepetition Swank
Agreement&#148;), was entered into on July&nbsp;1, 1999 and contains terms substantially
similar to those described above, except as follows: (a)&nbsp;the original term of
the agreement is for three years; (b)&nbsp;Mr.&nbsp;Swank agreed that he will not
voluntarily terminate his employment during the original term of the agreement
without good reason (or for certain other specified reasons); (c)&nbsp;the agreement
provides for specified bonus payments, which will be paid if Mr.&nbsp;Swank remains
employed, if he terminates employment for good reason or if he is terminated
without good cause; (d)&nbsp;Mr.&nbsp;Swank may terminate his employment and receive
severance pay if there is a change in the composition of Old Purina&#146;s Board of
Directors initiated by Koch Industries; (e)&nbsp;in certain circumstances, the
amount of severance pay can be as much as three times annual base pay, plus
three times the amount of the executive&#146;s annual bonus (subject to the
limitation imposed by section 280G of the Internal Revenue Code); and (f)&nbsp;the
non-compete provision only applies for one year. Koch Industries guaranteed
all of Old Purina&#146;s monetary obligations under Section&nbsp;4 of the Prepetition
Swank Agreement. In connection with certain agreements between the Creditors&#146;
Committee, Koch Industries and Mr.&nbsp;Swank, Old Purina obtained an order of the
Bankruptcy Court dated February&nbsp;16, 2000 (i)&nbsp;terminating the Prepetition Swank
Agreement and releasing all of Mr.&nbsp;Swank&#146;s claims thereunder against the Old
Purina Companies; (ii)&nbsp;authorizing Old Purina to enter into a new employment
agreement with Mr.&nbsp;Swank (the &#147;New Swank Agreement&#148;), which contains terms
substantially identical in form and substance to the Senior Executive
Agreements, and pay a signing bonus of $350,000 to Mr.&nbsp;Swank upon execution of
the New Swank Agreement; and (iii)&nbsp;terminating a guarantee of all monetary
obligations under Section&nbsp;4 of the Prepetition Swank Agreement by Koch
Industries and releasing all claims thereunder in exchange for a settlement
payment from Koch Industries to Mr.&nbsp;Swank in the amount of $350,000. Old
Purina and Mr.&nbsp;Swank entered into the New Swank Agreement effective February
16, 2000.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<B><I>New Benefit Programs</I></B>

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Reorganized Purina will implement the following new benefit plan:

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;<I>Equity Incentive Plan.</I>&nbsp;The Equity Incentive Plan in many respects will
replace certain elements of the KERP Program as Reorganized Purina&#146;s long-term
incentive and retention arrangement. It currently is anticipated that other
elements of the KERP Program, such as the annual incentive program and the
special project bonus plan would continue after the Effective Date.
Reorganized Purina&#146;s Board of Directors (or a committee thereof) will determine
the awards to be granted under the Equity Incentive Plan. The Equity Incentive
Plan will provide for grants of stock options to the employees and members of
the Board of Directors of Reorganized Purina. A total of one million shares of
Common Stock will be available for issuance in satisfaction of awards under the
Equity Incentive Plan, of which grants for certain shares will be made by
Reorganized Purina&#146;s new Board of Directors, or a committee thereof, within 45
days after the Effective Date.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Following the 1998 Merger, Old Purina entered into an exclusive commodity
purchasing agreement (the &#147;Master Procurement Agreement&#148;) with Koch
Agriculture. Under the terms of the Master Procurement Agreement, Koch
Agriculture&#146;s Nutrient Services Division agreed to supply Old Purina with its
requirements for feed ingredients, feed additives and feed packaging materials.
For the year ended December&nbsp;31 1999, Old Purina purchased approximately $449.5
million in commodities from Koch Agriculture&#146;s Nutrient Services Division. See
&#147;Risk Factors &#151; Integration of Commodity Purchasing and Other Business
Functions.&#148;

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Since the 1998 Merger, Old Purina contracted with Koch Industries for
numerous administrative and support services, including all payroll systems and
most employee benefit programs through December&nbsp;31, 1999. See &#147;Executive
Compensation &#151; Employee Benefit Matters &#151; Existing Benefit Programs.&#148; For the
year ended December&nbsp;31 1999, the total fees paid in connection with such
services amounted to $3.5&nbsp;million. In addition, commencing in May&nbsp;1998, Koch
Industries began administering and funding all of Old Purina&#146;s employee
payroll, benefit and related costs, for which it was to be reimbursed by Old
Purina. Beginning in late October&nbsp;1998, Old Purina began to reimburse Koch
Industries periodically for such advances. In late October and November&nbsp;1998,
Old Purina reimbursed Koch Industries approximately $53&nbsp;million for payroll and
associated employee benefit costs

<H5 align="left"><A HREF="#toc">Table of Contents</A></H5><P>


<P>relating to the period from May&nbsp;1998 through
September&nbsp;1998. See &#147;Risk Factors &#151; Integration of Commodity Purchasing and
Other Business Functions.&#148;

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Two tax sharing agreements were executed effective as of the date of the
1998 Merger: (a)&nbsp;the Parent Tax Sharing Agreement (the &#147;Parent Tax Sharing
Agreement&#148;), between Koch Industries and PM Holdings and (b)&nbsp;the Sub-Group Tax
Sharing Agreement (the &#147;Sub-Group Tax Sharing Agreement&#148;), between PM Holdings
and each of its subsidiaries (including Old Purina). The Parent Tax Sharing
Agreement provides that the federal income tax liability of the entire Koch
Industries consolidated group (including the Old Purina Companies) will be
allocated between the aggregate Koch Entities and Old Purina on the basis of
the percentage that each group&#146;s total tax, hypothetically computed as if each
group were a separate consolidated group, would bear to the total of the
hypothetically-computed taxes. If the hypothetical computation yielded a loss
for the aggregate Old Purina Companies, (i)&nbsp;the Old Purina Companies would have
no liability to Koch Industries for income taxes in that year and would be
permitted to take the loss into account in a later tax year when the loss could
be used on a stand-alone basis and (ii)&nbsp;Koch Industries would have no
obligation to make a cash payment to the Old Purina Companies for the benefit
of such loss. The Sub-Group Tax Sharing Agreement provided an identical method
for sharing any liability of the Old Purina Companies under the Parent Tax
Sharing Agreement among the Old Purina Companies. The results of operations of
Old Purina after March&nbsp;12, 1998 have been included in the consolidated federal
corporate income tax return and certain consolidated state income tax returns
of Koch Industries. Under the Koch Tax Sharing Agreement (which will be signed
in connection with PMI Merger but will be effective for most, but not all
purposes on the Effective Date), the following will occur: (a)&nbsp;the parties to
the Parent Tax Sharing Agreement will waive all claims that they might have
under that Agreement (which will be superseded by the Koch Tax Sharing
Agreement); (b)&nbsp;Koch Industries and Reorganized Purina will indemnify each
other for any taxes owed by the other for periods during which Old Purina was
not part of the Koch Industries consolidated group; (c)&nbsp;Koch Industries will
indemnify Reorganized Purina for any taxes associated with the PMI Merger; and
(d)&nbsp;Reorganized Purina will indemnify Koch Industries for certain tax
liabilities arising on audit to the extent that those liabilities would have
been due and payable by Reorganized Purina had it never been a member of the
Koch Industries consolidated group. See &#147;Risk Factors &#151; Federal Income Tax.&#148;

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In October&nbsp;1999, Old Purina entered into employment agreements with
Messrs.&nbsp;Dumler, Durkin and Knudson in their capacity as members of the Office
of the Chief Executive Officer (collectively, the &#147;OCEO Agreements&#148;). The OCEO
Agreements provided that these executives will receive an annual salary of
$250,000, of which $100,000 has been paid by Old Purina and the remainder has
been paid by Koch Industries, and is eligible for annual incentive payments and
emergence bonuses under the KERP Program. The OCEO Agreements also set forth
each executive&#146;s right to receive severance pay in the amount of $350,000 if
(a)&nbsp;the executive&#146;s employment with Old Purina was terminated without cause and
the executive is not offered a position with the Koch Entities that is
equivalent to or better than the position previously held by the executive
prior to his assuming responsibilities at Old Purina or (b)&nbsp;the executive
terminates his employment with Old Purina and accepts a position with the Koch
Entities that is equivalent to or better than the position previously held by
the executive prior to assuming responsibilities at Old Purina and, within two
years thereafter, the executive&#146;s employment is terminated either (i)&nbsp;by the
Koch Entities without cause or (ii)&nbsp;voluntarily by the executive as a result of
a reduction in his role with or compensation from the Koch Entities.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In accordance with certain agreements with the Creditors&#146; Committee and
the bank group under the Prepetition Credit Facility, Old Purina determined not
to pursue its request for authority to assume the OCEO Agreements and instead
obtained an order of the Bankruptcy Court dated January&nbsp;18, 2000 under which,
among other things, (a)&nbsp;the OCEO Agreements were rejected as of March&nbsp;1, 2000
(the &#147;OCEO Rejection Date&#148;); (b)&nbsp;as of the OCEO Rejection Date, Messrs.&nbsp;Dumler,
Durkin and Knudson were each entitled to (i)&nbsp;a cash severance payment equal to
$250,000 and (ii)&nbsp;a general unsecured claim of $100,000 under the Plan; (c)
Messrs.&nbsp;Dumler, Durkin and Knudson continue to serve as members of Old
Purina&#146;s Board of Directors through the Effective Date without additional
compensation; and (d)&nbsp;notwithstanding the rejection of the OCEO Agreements
prior to the Confirmation Date, Messrs.&nbsp;Dumler, Durkin and Knudson were
entitled to their emergence bonuses and other payments under the KERP Program
on the terms described above. As of February&nbsp;4, 2000, the three-member Office
of the Chief Executive Officer was eliminated, and Messrs.&nbsp;Dumler, Durkin and
Knudson no longer serve in that capacity.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In October&nbsp;1999, Old Purina entered into a Transition Services Agreement

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;On November&nbsp;9, 1999, Koch Industries, Koch Agriculture and the holders
(collectively, the &#147;Consenting Holders&#148;) of approximately 55% of the principal
amount of the Senior Subordinated Notes entered into an agreement (the
&#147;November Settlement&#148;) with respect to Old Purina&#146;s restructuring and the
resolution of potential claims by and against Koch Industries, Koch Agriculture
and their affiliates. Old Purina was not a party to the November Settlement.
Pursuant to the November Settlement, the Consenting Holders agreed not to vote
in favor of a plan of reorganization for Old Purina unless such plan
incorporated certain provisions set forth therein. In late December&nbsp;1999, Old
Purina, Koch Industries and the Creditors&#146; Committee met and reached further
agreements regarding certain disputes and issues that had arisen under the
November Settlement and in connection with the Transition Services Agreement
(the &#147;December Settlement&#148;). The Plan constitutes the agreement among Koch
Industries, Koch Agriculture, the Creditors&#146; Committee, the Consenting
Noteholders and Old Purina regarding the settlement of issues among the Koch
Entities, Old Purina and Old Purina&#146;s creditors. As of February&nbsp;14, 2000, Koch
Industries, Koch Agriculture and the Consenting Holders entered into certain
new agreements pursuant to which the Consenting Holders agreed to vote in favor
of the Plan, subject to the satisfaction of certain conditions.

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In December&nbsp;1999, Old Purina entered into a Supplemental Transition
Agreement with Koch Industries and Koch Agriculture (the &#147;Supplemental
Transition Agreement&#148;). Under the Supplemental Transition Agreement, the Koch
Entities agreed to cooperate in the transition of certain employee benefit and
commodity purchasing functions to Old Purina. Among other things, the Koch
Entities have agreed to (i)&nbsp;continue providing certain retiree medical
benefits, (ii)&nbsp;transfer certain commodity supply contracts, (iii)&nbsp;provide
incentives to certain Koch Agriculture employees involved in the commodity
program to return to Old Purina, (iv)&nbsp;transfer commodity purchasing operations
to Old Purina and (v)&nbsp;transfer files and software licenses and cooperatively
install computer systems related to commodity purchasing activities. Pursuant
to the Plan, Reorganized Purina will pay Koch Industries $1.57&nbsp;million in
consideration for the Supplemental Transition Agreement. See &#147;Risk Factors &#151;
Integration of Commodity Purchasing and Other Business Functions.&#148;

<P>&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;In connection with the consummation of PMI Merger, Koch Agriculture will
be granted an option to purchase the Warrant pursuant to a warrant purchase
agreement (&#147;the Warrant Purchase Agreement&#148;). Under the Warrant Purchase
Agreement, Koch Agriculture will have the right, during the period commencing
immediately after consummation of the PMI Merger and ending on the Effective
Date, to purchase the Warrant from PM Holdings for $5.0&nbsp;million. Pursuant to
the terms of the Warrant and the Warrant Purchase Agreement governing the terms
and conditions of the Warrant, Koch Agriculture will have the right for one
year after the Effective Date to purchase shares of Common Stock comprising up
to 10% of the aggregate amount of Common Stock outstanding as of the Effective
Date, on a fully diluted basis, at a purchase price of $27.75 per share. See
&#147;Business &#151; Bankruptcy&#148; and &#147;Recent Sales of Unregistered Securities.&#148;
